newsitem.title: AZERBAIJAN: FEATURE - Hitting the comeback trail in Azerbaijan.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hitting the comeback trail in Azerbaijan.

text.p: Albufaz Elchibey takes his time over interviews, punctuating raspy words with long drags on Marlboro cigarettes.

Time is something Elchibey, Azerbaijan's first democratically elected president, has had plenty of for the past four years, after fleeing a military revolt into internal exile in a remote region of this former Soviet republic.

Now the rail-thin, bearded former professor says he is preparing to leave his mountain hideaway for the capital Baku and is even pondering a challenge to current leader Haydar Aliyev in a planned 1998 presidential contest.
"I must return to Baku and to political life. It could be in two months or three months, but I will return," he told Reuters in the Nakhchivan Autonomous Region, 600 km (350 miles) from the capital.

While his detractors dismiss him as a has-been, some observers say his impact on Azerbaijan's unpredictable political scene could be substantial. And political clout here means big stakes these days - a chance to control huge oil reserves.
ELCHIBEY HAD DRAMATIC DEMISE
Elchibey's rule was short-lived. In 1992 he was elected overwhelmingly on a heady wave of anti-communist nationalism sweeping former Soviet republics.

But just one year later the ardent nationalist was forced out after key army officers refused to defend Baku against an uprising by rebel troops based in the west of the country led by shadowy businessman Suret Huseinov.
Elchibey still claims the uprising was inspired by circles in Russia incensed at his insistence that Russian troops leave their military bases in Azerbaijan. Moscow denies the charges.
He was replaced by former Soviet-era Azeri strongman Haydar Aliyev, at first "temporarily" and then until 1998, after Aliyev called new elections.
Elchibey meanwhile, continued to consider himself the legal president but was stuck in Keleki, afraid to return to Baku having been blamed for the bloodshed in fighting with Huseinov.

Aliyev, 74, has since reasserted pre-eminence over almost every aspect of political life in the former Soviet republic of eight million. Giant portraits of the one-time Soviet politburo member and his most famous quotes adorn many a street corner.

"I still consider myself the legal President of Azerbaijan, despite the fact that de facto power is in the hands of Haydar Aliyev. Since I was removed from office by a revolt, I do not consider this legal," he said.
PROSPECTS FOR A COMEBACK
Dismissing charges that he is washed up politically, Elchibey says he may challenge Aliyev in a 1998 presidential vote. Aliyev is almost certain to seek re-election.

"If conditions are democratic, I will take part as a candidate," he said. Democratic congress, an alliance of seven opposition parties which includes Elchibey's Popular Front, has joined ranks and says it will present a united candidate in 1998, quite possibly Elchibey.
While most in Aliyev's ruling New Azerbaijan bloc scoff at Elchibey's chances, some political observers say his impact could be far from minimal.

They point to the fact that Aliyev, while believed to enjoy wide popularity, faced no serious opposition in his 1993 election. A 1995 parliamentary election that gave his party a huge majority was regarded as flawed by foreign monitors.
"Although to many Elchibey may be a figure of yesterday, I've learned that Azeri politics are just too unpredictable to say what might happen," said one Western diplomat.

"Aliyev would probably win at least 65 percent of the vote if the election were held today. But we just don't know how to really gauge the public mood because there have never been truly open and fair elections," he said.

The stakes are far from miniscule. Once an unknown outpost of the Soviet Union, the republic has signed $18 billion in contracts with foreign firms to develop its massive offshore Caspian Sea oil reserves. More are in the works.

So far the deals, announced with great fanfare, have not meant prosperity for average Azeris, the majority of whom still live below the poverty line. If public discontent can be tapped, observers say, Aliyev could be vulnerable.

While Aliyev's government is decidedly pro-Western, it has tried to balance its orientation towards the West -- and the awarding of lucrative oil development contracts -- by including Russia and Iran even as ties continued to be strained with both.

Diplomats say Elchibey would probably be far more openly pro-Turkish and pro-western and would take a hostile line towards Iran, which he accuses of wanting to destroy predominantly Moslem Azerbaijan's secular way of life.
HOW ALIYEV'S GOVERNMENT WOULD REACT
"I don't want my return to be an occasion for instability. I don't want to push the country into a bad position. I would like to help Azerbaijan to develop civil harmony," Elchibey vows.
But recent comments by the country's chief prosecutor in two government-run newspapers have given the impression that he might be unwelcome in Baku.

"Elchibey's actions after (Aliyev's election in 1993) violate not only ethical, but also the criminal and civil norms of the country," said Eldar Gasanov, refering to sections of the country's legal code dealing with the unlawful seizure of power and misrepresenting oneself as president.
"This is the best evidence that Aliyev is still afraid of Albufaz Elchibey," said Asim Molzade, a Popular Front leader.
